title: ALIGNAgent: Adaptive Learner Intelligence for Gap Identification and Next-step guidance
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that many personalized learning systems in education are fragmented: some estimate student knowledge, others diagnose misconceptions, and others recommend resources, but few connect these functions into a continuous adaptive cycle. The authors aim to build and evaluate a unified AI-based framework that can use student assessment data to estimate topic proficiency, identify concept-level skill gaps, and recommend targeted next-step learning resources before students move on to new material.

The proposed intervention is ALIGNAgent, a multi-agent educational framework composed primarily of a Skill Gap Agent, a Recommender Agent, and a Summary Agent. The system processes learner preference survey data, gradebook records, and question-level quiz responses to compute topic-level proficiency scores, diagnose likely misconceptions using concept tags and incorrect answer patterns, and retrieve preference-aware learning materials through web search. The framework also generates learner-facing summaries that explain strengths, weaknesses, and suggested next actions. The empirical evaluation compares model-generated knowledge proficiency estimates and difficulty labels against instructor judgments and actual student exam performance, using precision, recall, F1, and accuracy.

The population consisted of undergraduate students in two computer science courses at Florida Polytechnic University in the United States: COP3415 (Data Structures; 14 students) and CDA2108 (Fundamentals of Computer Systems; 11 students), both offered in Summer 2025. The study used authentic classroom data including quizzes, midterm and final exam scores, and self-reported learning preferences. The context was regular higher-education coursework at a single university, with midterm and final exam outcomes treated as the ground truth for validating model inferences.

The main conclusion is that ALIGNAgent shows promising effectiveness for AI-supported personalized learning in higher education. According to the abstract and reported results, GPT-4o-based agents achieved strong performance in knowledge proficiency estimation, with precision of 0.87-0.90 and F1 scores of 0.84-0.87 when validated against actual exam performance. GPT-4o also outperformed Claude 3.5 Sonnet and LLaMA 3 in question difficulty labeling across both courses. Overall, the authors argue that a coordinated multi-agent pipeline can provide interpretable diagnosis, targeted recommendations, and a practical closed-loop approach to adaptive learning, though the evidence comes from a small, single-institution sample.

identified_tools.name: ALIGNAgent
identified_tools.description: A proposed multi-agent personalized learning framework that integrates knowledge estimation, skill-gap identification, resource recommendation, and summary feedback using LLM-based agents.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an adaptive higher-education learning system using quiz performance, gradebook data, and learner preferences from two undergraduate computer science courses to estimate topic proficiency, identify concept-level gaps, and recommend targeted resources; GPT-4o-, Claude 3.5-, and LLaMA 3-based agent configurations were compared.

findings.finding_summary: On two authentic undergraduate computer science course datasets, ALIGNAgent with GPT-4o-based agents achieved precision of 0.87-0.90 and F1 scores of 0.84-0.87 for knowledge proficiency estimation, validated against actual exam performance. The abstract reports these results as evidence of effective knowledge proficiency estimation, though full per-dataset sample-linked breakdowns are not provided in the excerpt.
findings.measure: Knowledge proficiency estimation performance against actual exam performance (precision, F1)

findings.finding_summary: For question difficulty labeling used within the ALIGNAgent pipeline, GPT-4o produced the strongest reported performance among compared models. In COP3415, GPT-4o achieved precision 0.81, recall 0.53, F1 0.61, accuracy 0.52; in CDA2108, it achieved precision 0.88, recall 0.61, F1 0.72, accuracy 0.63.
findings.measure: Question difficulty labeling performance (precision, recall, F1, accuracy)
findings.effect_size: COP3415: precision=0.81, recall=0.53, F1=0.61, accuracy=0.52; CDA2108: precision=0.88, recall=0.61, F1=0.72, accuracy=0.63

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical evaluation on authentic course datasets, but the study appears to be a non-randomized system evaluation with small samples from two undergraduate courses (14 and 11 students) rather than an RCT or strong causal design.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising precision/F1 performance for proficiency estimation and labeling accuracy, but does not report student learning gains, standardized effect sizes, or causal impacts on outcomes, so practical impact remains encouraging but unclear.
